rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — the country has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. The country's two main cities have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: a human-rights organisation documents "shocking" harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially. The consequence axis of an arrest is thinly documented and cannot be read as a protected standard: the only placement finding is a February 2025 statement by the president of the national human-rights committee, made in praise of a women's correctional facility, that transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from the men's facility to the women's facility — a surgery-gated practice with no statute or formal policy text cited. Nothing is documented on placement for trans prisoners who have not had surgery, and no trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is on record; with no legal gender recognition, a detained trans visitor's placement would default to birth sex absent the surgery-gated transfer — a gap that cannot be assumed safe even though the country's non-criminalising framework keeps arrest itself unlikely.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The cooperative posture carries an unfulfilled-promise edge: the country also accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage (2019 review) and seven on marriage equality (2024 review), and legislation still contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions — a reform-promise layer rather than a visitor-facing restriction.

The same report flags that prison overcrowding has worsened because of gang-crackdown arrests — the custody context in which any placement decision would operate, resident-facing rather than a visitor-facing restriction.

The LGR absence and discrimination-law gaps are resident-facing; a local police extortion practice primarily affects resident trans women.

The documented harassment and abuse cases describe resident trans women on city streets, and the police practice of targeting resident trans sex workers is the sharpest resident-facing manifestation.

The custody findings are resident-facing: the surgery-gated transfer practice at a correctional facility and the worsened overcrowding from gang-crackdown arrests describe the national prison system — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.

The police-practice reports are reported but not adjudicated by any court in this record; the expert-visit findings are summarised from the hosting organisation's page and not independently re-verified here. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is dangerous for trans visitors. A penal code from 1883 criminalises same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and a human-rights trust lists the country as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. An international commission of jurists identifies the national police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. The capital has a small organised community and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.

The consequence axis makes the danger concrete: as of October 2024 the national prison authority has no dedicated transgender housing — its media spokesperson/Commissioner said current facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, with separate accommodation only planned for prisons built in the future — and placement defaults to birth sex in the current male/female ward system, with a discretionary, medicalised exception route: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender ‘where possible’, while those without it undergo a doctor’s assessment of whether they ‘can be considered a transgender’ before placement, with the inmate’s preference weighed. Officials also cite the fear of people accused of sex offences ‘identifying as transgender’ to enter female housing with born-male offenders as a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. A detained trans visitor — unlikely to hold the recognition card, in a country where police already use vagrancy and personation provisions against trans people — would default to birth-sex placement under a practice with no statutory rule and no dedicated housing.

Placement-framework context: a prisoners'-rights committee is calling for future prisons to give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that ‘developed countries have recognised transgender rights’ — advocacy positioning around the documented birth-sex default rather than a visitor-facing protection.

The custody findings are resident-facing: the birth-sex placement default, the ID-gated ‘where possible’ preference route, the doctor’s-assessment path for detainees without the recognition card, and the officials’ articulated concern about sex-offence suspects ‘identifying as transgender’ to enter female housing with born-male offenders — all govern residents held in the country's prisons; a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is dangerous for trans visitors. A criminal buggery statute (up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of a regional human-rights commission case documenting official failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resort areas are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.

The consequence axis of an arrest is directly documented. A 2018 academic study of the country's prisons — estimating that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at the main adult correctional centre belong to sexual or gender minorities — reported that prisoners perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender ‘are isolated’, that rehabilitation opportunities are ‘basically non-existent’, that homophobia/transphobia is entrenched (other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners), and that lesbians face prevalent ‘corrective rape’. A national government's 2023 report confirms the institutional dimension: ‘prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity’, in facilities so overcrowded that maximum-security cells at the main centre held three times capacity, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The country bars legal gender registration, no specialised trans housing policy is documented, and for a detained trans visitor this is identity-targeted violence on top of an already severe, overcrowded baseline — a documented tier of its own, not merely an elevated version of a general prison risk.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The buggery law (up to 10 years) is a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners and shapes police culture.

Litigation flux: the proceeding before the regional human-rights commission — whose February 2024 amicus brief argued the country's continued criminalisation and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — is the official-failure pattern the prison documentation extends: the same authorities that failed to investigate a mob killing hold trans prisoners without a recognition framework or documented protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:

The custody findings govern residents held in custody: the 2018 study’s documentation of isolation, curtailed movement, limited access to resources and ‘corrective rape’, and the national government's reporting of identity-targeted prisoner-on-prisoner violence in overcrowded facilities — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.

The buggery law is a situational/climate factor; resort vs. non-resort risk differs sharply.

Prison axis: the 300-of-1,800 estimate for the main adult correctional centre and the ‘corrective rape’ prevalence claim are study-reported figures not independently re-verified here; the national government's report documents severity but not the identity-targeting share of overall prison violence; no specialised trans housing policy, trans special unit, or solitary/segregation policy is documented; and with gender registration barred, no recognition framework governs accommodation decisions.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the historic-era buggery laws (a 2018 ruling, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of dating-app ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.

The consequence axis of an arrest is acknowledged in official terms as unsafe: a 2018 gender-equality protocol for judicial officers states plainly that ‘in this country, there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities’. The only mechanism is a judicial officer’s sentencing recommendation that prison authorities make provisions for the inmate’s physical safety, and the protocol’s other directives — courts to refer to intersex/transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and permit court access irrespective of dress — govern court process rather than custody placement. Placement for a detained trans visitor is therefore discretionary, with no dedicated facility, special unit or statutory placement standard on record; the documented official position is that the penal system cannot safely accommodate trans prisoners.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The dating-app ambush robbery pattern is a direct risk for trans visitors using apps.

Placement-framework context: the protocol was a justice-sector initiative launched in November 2018 by a regional court of justice, a regional judicial organisation, a UN women's agency, a legal-reform project, a national association of women judges and a national judicial institute — institutional recognition of the custody gap rather than a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
No LGR and no SOGI anti-discrimination protection — resident-facing; the “beaten, stoned and chopped” pattern describes residents.

The custody findings govern residents held in custody: the absence of special facilities for persons with non-traditional gender identities and the sentencing-recommendation mechanism are national prison/court practice — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Decriminalisation status and reform rejections are climate/legal context; no trans-specific statute exists.

Prison axis: the protocol is a judicial-officers’ standard, not a statute — no trans-prisoner placement rule, dedicated facility, special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is on record; how prison authorities actually respond to sentencing recommendations is undocumented; and the protocol dates from November 2018 with no implementation evidence in this record.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is dangerous for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed a human sexual rights and family values bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for “promotion.” The president refused to assent pending legal challenges, the nation's top court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when the 8th parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected. That reintroduction materialised in late May 2026, when parliament passed a new human sexual rights and family values bill: up to three years’ imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, longer terms for promotion/advocacy, and a ‘duty to report’ prohibited acts to police — passed under pressure from religious leaders on the president, whose ratification is still required and widely expected.

Under existing law, “unnatural carnal knowledge” carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The capital has a resilient underground community (a local LGBT-rights organisation — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.

The consequence axis of an arrest is the direct official pathway this bill creates: if ratified, identity alone becomes an imprisonable offence for the population that any prison-placement practice would apply to. Neither the 2026 reporting nor any source in this record contains a provision on how such prisoners would be housed, and no national prison placement rule, trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is publicly documented. In a country that criminalises identity and lacks legal gender recognition, with documented mob violence, an undocumented placement practice cannot be assumed safe: a detained trans visitor would be held under a system with no documented housing standard and no documented recourse.
rewrites.blindTangential:
“Unnatural carnal knowledge” (up to 3 years) criminalises same-sex conduct — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the lapsed bill would have criminalised identity itself.

Political-process context: the May 2026 passage came under pressure from religious leaders on the president, whose ratification is still required; the new bill carries the same name and identity-criminalising structure as the lapsed 2024 bill, confirming the legislative trajectory the earlier unanimous passage signalled.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
Resident-facing: there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection; mob justice against perceived LGBT people falls on residents; the resilient underground community (a local LGBT-rights organisation — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks) reflects resident organising; and the 2026 reports of panic, eviction risk and self-censorship among local community groups describe residents.

If the 2026 bill is ratified, its imprisonment exposure and ‘duty to report’ fall first on residents who are visibly or known to be LGBTQ+; the absence of any publicly documented trans-prisoner housing policy is a gap that residents held in custody would stand under — a visitor meets the custody system only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
The 2024 bill never became law (lapsed unassented); its significance is climate/trajectory.

Prison axis: the May 2026 bill’s ratification status is unresolved in the sources — parliament passed it on 29-30 May 2026 and the president had not yet accepted as of the reporting, which expected his signature — and must be rechecked; neither the 2024 nor the 2026 text, as reported, contains any provision on how trans prisoners would be housed; and no national prison placement rule, trans special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is documented in any source in this record.
